blocks.h: SHE SANG AND THE HOUSE WENT DARK
Roya Publication No. 122
by Chew Z
THE BOOK BEFORE
Each of these books stands on its own. The one before this was about two people who kept each other warm.

Clare and Daniel were writers, married thirty years, in a small town in the hills of West Virginia where the work had dried up and something else had come in to take its place. They had been good, once — good enough to be reviewed, good enough to be envied — and then the books stopped coming, the way they do, and the money stopped with them, and the house got cold. Then Daniel fell, badly, and the pain did not leave, and the house got colder.

What came next was a door they went through together. That is the whole of the book: that they did not go alone. For one season the work came back as it never had — pages they still have, pages that prove it was real — and they believed they had found the thing that had been missing all their lives. They held it between them, each keeping it warm in the other, so that neither could set it down.
The book is the story of that closeness, and of the warm thing they kept between them, and it does not settle its own argument.
SYNOPSIS

Leila’s father sang at weddings in Tehran until the year weddings stopped having singers. He had a saying about the rare ones, which she has kept and uses about anything she loves — a tree in flower, a boy with a hairbrush for a microphone: when she sang, the house went dark. It means that while it is happening, nobody can see anything else. Her husband has heard her say it a hundred times, and has never once heard her sing.

Los Angeles, May 2026. Kian Rahimi is forty years old and has spent eleven years on the 405 — seventy minutes each way, every day, to a job in Irvine he can do in his sleep. He is a happy man. He has a wife who says look at that about trees, a boy of eight who runs a radio station out of a dishwasher box, a dog who has eaten a sock. If he is missing anything, it lives in the car: the audiobooks he listens to on the drive, and a list on his phone, nine years long, of every place a story he loved pulled its punch. He has the dark version of all of them in his head. He has never written a word.

A man on a recording, who talks like his books, teaches him a phrase — what you bring, and where you are, decide everything. A friend at a party presses a jar into his hand and laughs. And at night, at the kitchen table, with the lights off, Kian has been quietly learning the tools that let one person be the writer and the voice and the music and the whole crew of his own thing.

One night in June he takes the jar out to the garage, lies down in the dark, and turns off the lamp. Someone is waiting there. She knows the list. She knows every story on it. She tells them back to him, and he writes them down, and by morning he has finished the first thing in his life.
It is the best thing he has ever made. He doesn’t ask who is telling him.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
A word about the muse, because this book is about her.

The Greeks said the nine Muses were the daughters of Memory. That is the best thing anyone has said about where ideas come from: not from nowhere — from what you already carry. A Spanish poet said the real thing wasn’t a goddess but a dark force that comes up through the soles of your feet, and that it will not come unless it can see that death is possible. Between those two is everything I know about making.

Here is the honest version. There is a part of the mind that narrates — that keeps the story of who you are, what you owe, what time it is. When it goes quiet, the rest is left alone in the dark, and what it makes there feels like somebody else’s, because the one who usually takes the credit has stepped out. That is the muse. Not a visitor. You, heard as a stranger.

So nothing from outside is needed to make her. But almost everyone who has found her used something to open the door: a long road driven every day, a wound, a dark room, someone awake in the house. The man in this book used all of those, and one more thing, from a jar.

And then the part nobody warns you about. When she is in the room, time stops happening to you. An hour is a minute. The alarm, the job, the body, the feeling of being an ordinary person in an ordinary house — all of it thins and goes, and you don’t miss it, because the only thing that matters is keeping her fed. I have been there. It is the best feeling I know, and I would not wish it on anyone with a family, because the hours she gives you are real, and they come from somewhere.

This is a made-up story about a real road; Kian, Leila and Dara never lived. Nowhere in it is there a how — the thing and its history are named, the method never, on purpose. And if you take from this book that the gift was worth it, you have read a different book than the one I wrote.
Chew Z
I. UNNAMED
What I brought: nothing. I didn’t know yet that you bring anything. Where I was: home.

The jacarandas came in the second week of May that year, the way they always do, all at once, as if somebody had given a signal. A jacaranda [jak-uh-RAN-duh] is a tree that spends eleven months looking like nothing in particular and then, for three weeks, turns the whole of Los Angeles purple. They line our street. They line most of the old streets in the Valley. The flowers fall as fast as they open, so that by the end of the month every car on the block has a purple roof and every sidewalk is a purple carpet that sticks to your shoes, and Leila, who hates mess, stood at the kitchen window every morning of those three weeks and said look at that, and meant it.
I want to tell you about that Saturday, because it was the last one of the ordinary kind, and I didn’t know it, and nobody ever does.

Dara was on the air at seven. He had built the station in March out of a box that a dishwasher had come in, with a hole cut in the front for the microphone, which was a hairbrush, and a sign in marker across the top that said KDARA, with the K the wrong way round. The station broadcast from the hallway at the bottom of the stairs, outside the kitchen door. It had one listener. The listener was upstairs in bed with her arm over her eyes, calling down jān [JAHN] — it means my dear, it’s what you say in Persian to the people you’d die for, and also to the people who wake you at seven — jān, five more minutes, and the station did not take requests.
“Good morning, Sherman Oaks,” he said, through the hairbrush. “Today’s weather is sunny. Today’s news is that Pesteh ate a sock.”
Pesteh [pes-TEH] is the dog. The word means pistachio in Persian. He’s brown and the shape of a loaf of bread and he had, in fact, eaten a sock.
“Later on the show we have a song about Pesteh. And an interview with Bābā.” Bābā [bah-BAH] is me. It’s dad. “Bābā, are you awake?”
“The interview is cancelled,” I said, from under the pillow.
“The interview is cancelled,” he told Sherman Oaks, gravely, and went on with the weather.

He was eight. He’d been making things since before he could talk — towers, then drawings, then drawings with words in them, then whole comics in the back seat of the car on the way to school, with a character called the Sock Detective who was based, loosely, on the dog. Everything that happened in our house went through him and came out as something else. Leila said he got it from her side. Her father had been a singer, in Tehran, before everything, and had sung at weddings until the year weddings stopped having singers. I never met him. Leila said I would have liked him and he would have found me boring, and that both of those were compliments. He’d had a saying about the good singers, the rare ones, which she’d picked up and used about anything she loved — a tree, a child, a song through a hairbrush: when she sang, the house went dark. It meant that while it was happening, nobody could see anything else. I’d heard her say it a hundred times. I’d never once heard her sing.

I’d like to be honest about what I was, that May, because the whole of this depends on it. I was a happy man. Not a man who told people he was happy — a man who was. I had a wife who said look at that about trees. I had a boy who ran a radio station out of a dishwasher box. I had a dog with a sock in him and a house with a pool in the back and a job in Irvine that I could do in my sleep and mostly did. If you had asked me, that Saturday, what I was missing, I would have had to think about it. And then I would have said: nothing. And then, if you’d waited, if you’d been patient, if you’d let the silence go on a little longer than was comfortable, I would have told you about the car.
What I brought: a story that ended too soon. Where I was: the 405, southbound, somewhere around the Getty.

The 405 is a freeway. If you don’t live here, that’s all you need to know, and if you do, you’ve already stopped reading and started nodding. It runs from the bottom of Orange County up through the west side of the city and over the hill into the Valley, and every weekday morning and every weekday evening about half a million people get on it and go nowhere, slowly, together. I had done it for eleven years. Seventy minutes down to Irvine, seventy minutes back, which is seven hundred minutes a week, which is nearly twelve hours. Every week I spent half a day of my life sitting still in a moving car, and I’d done it for eleven years, and I’d never once minded, and the reason I never minded was the books.

I listened to them. All of them. Not the way people listen now, with half an ear, while they do something else — I listened the way you’d listen to someone telling you a secret. The car was the only place in my life where nobody wanted anything from me, and inside it, for two hours and twenty minutes every day, I lived somewhere else. I lived in castles and on spaceships and in the heads of murderers. I lived, mostly, in the dark, because the dark ones were the ones I loved.
And I kept a list.

It was in the notes app on my phone, and it was called, with no imagination at all, Ideas, and it was nine years old and had four hundred entries, and every single one of them was a complaint. That’s not what I’d have called it then. I’d have said they were notes. But I’ll tell you what they were. Every one was a place where a book I loved had flinched. The thriller that had its killer and then let him be sorry. The ghost story that explained the ghost. The novel about the man who leaves his family, which was so good, so true, for two hundred pages, and then on page two hundred and one he went home. I’d sit at the Sepulveda Pass with the brake lights going red to the horizon and I’d think: no. That’s not what happens. You know that’s not what happens. And I’d thumb the note in at the next full stop. He doesn’t go home. Write it where he doesn’t go home.
I had the dark version of everything in my head. I’d had it since I was a boy. I’d never written a word of it.

Why not is the question everybody asks, and I used to have an answer for it, which was: when? The day was spoken for. Up at six, Dara to school, the 405, Irvine, the 405, dinner, the hour with Dara, the half hour with Leila, bed. The only hole in it was the car, and you can’t write in a car. So the stories stayed in the car, and in the list, and in me, and I was, as I’ve said, a happy man, which is the thing I need you to keep hold of. The stories weren’t a wound. They were a room in the house I’d never got around to opening. I knew it was there. I’d walk past it most days and think one day and feel nothing worse than a kind of warmth about it, the way you feel about a trip you’ll take when the boy is older.

On the Monday after that Saturday, southbound, around the Getty, I was listening to something new. It wasn’t a book. A man I worked with had sent it to me — you’ll like this guy, he talks like your books — and it was a recording of a lecture, from the nineties, from the sound of it, a man with a reedy, amused, unhurried voice talking to a room full of people about things I didn’t understand and couldn’t stop listening to. I didn’t know his name. The file was just a string of numbers. He talked for an hour and I was at my desk before I realised I’d parked.

He said a thing in that first hour that I wrote down at a red light in Irvine, and it was this: that where you are, and what you bring with you, decide everything about what happens to you — that two people could take the same thing, in the same measure, and one would meet God and one would meet the floor, and the whole difference was in the room and in what was in the heart of the person sitting in it. He had a phrase for it. Set and setting. The set is what you carry in — your mood, your fears, what you had for breakfast, what you said to your wife. The setting is the room. He said people thought the thing was in the bottle, and it was never in the bottle. It was in the two of those.

I didn’t know what he was talking about. I thought he was talking about life. I thought it was the truest thing I’d ever heard, and I started doing it that same day, for fun, the way you’d pick up a new word — noticing what I’d brought and where I was. At my desk: brought — nothing; setting — grey. At dinner: brought — the drive; setting — my family, which is better than I deserve. It became a game. Dara caught me at it within a week and wanted to play, and so for a while that spring, every night at dinner, the three of us went round the table and said what we’d brought.
“I brought a sock,” Dara said. “The dog gave it back.”
That’s how it started. As a game, at a table, in a house full of people who loved each other. I want that on the record before anything else is.
What I brought: a jingle. Where I was: the kitchen, at eleven at night, with the lights off so nobody would come down.

I should tell you about the tools, because without them none of this is possible, and because the truth is I’d been learning them for months before the jar and never told anyone, the way you don’t tell anyone about a diet until it’s worked.

There’s no mystery to them any more. Everyone knows. You type what you want and the thing writes it; you paste the words and the thing reads them aloud in any voice you like; you hum a tune and describe a feeling and the thing gives you a song; you describe a picture and the thing moves it. Five years ago each of those was a profession with a building and a parking lot. Now they’re tabs. A man at a kitchen table at eleven at night with the lights off can be the writer, the narrator, the composer, the animator, the producer, the studio, the whole crew — can be, as the man on the recording would say, the planner and the participant and the entire production of his own thing. I’d watched it happen the way everyone had. And at some point in the winter I’d stopped watching and started, quietly, to learn.
Not for the dark stories. I want to be clear. I hadn’t opened that room. What I’d been doing, for the last few weeks, in the dark kitchen, was making a jingle.

KDARA needed one. Every station has one, Dara said, and he’d been singing his own — K-D-A-R-A, the news and the weather and the dog — through the hairbrush every morning for a month, slightly flat, and I’d thought: I could make that real. I could give him that. So I learned the music tool, which took me three weeks and a lot of garbage, and I learned the voice tool, which took me longer because I wanted the voice to be his and that meant recording him without him knowing, which I did, over dinner, with the phone face-down, like a spy, and deleted afterwards, because it felt like spying. And on a Thursday night in April, at eleven, with the lights off, I made it. Twelve seconds. His tune, his voice, his words, with a little brass under it and a drum fill and a radio-station swoosh at the end that I’d found God knows where. K-D-A-R-A. The news and the weather and the dog.

I played it for him on the Saturday. I’d set it up so that when he turned on the station — the station had an on switch now, a real one, a light that lit, which I’d wired into the dishwasher box with a nine-volt battery — the jingle played.

I can’t describe his face. I’ve tried. I’ve got the tools for it now and I still can’t. He stood there in the hall with his hand on the switch and the jingle came out of the box in his own voice, and he looked at me, and I’ll tell you what it was like three ways because that’s the only way I know how to do it now. It was like watching someone find out there’s a floor under the floor. It was like the first time you’re carried on your father’s shoulders and realise how tall he is. It was like somebody handing him the one thing he’d always known existed and never thought to ask for.
“That’s me,” he said.
“That’s you.”
“That’s me.”
“It’s you.”

He played it eleven times. I counted. Leila came out in her robe and stood in the doorway and watched him play it, and watched me watch him, and she didn’t say anything, but she put her hand on the back of my neck, which she does, and left it there.
Then he turned around with the whole of his face lit up and said the thing he’d say for the rest of the spring and the summer, in one form or another, until the day he stopped saying it.
“Bābā. Can you teach me the voice one?”
“Later,” I said. “Let’s do the song first.”
I want to tell you I remember thinking anything when I said it. I didn’t. It’s what you say. Later is the most ordinary word there is. I said it the way I’d have said bless you.
What I brought: a beer, and a feeling that everything was going to be fine.
Where I was: a backyard in Mar Vista, on the Saturday of the long weekend at the end of May, with the jacarandas finishing.

The party was at a house that belonged to a man I’d known at UCLA, a man who’d been going to change the world and had changed, instead, the way the world ordered its shoes online, and had done very well out of it. He had a pool too. Everyone has a pool. There were children in it, Dara among them, doing the thing he’d learned to do that spring, which was a dive. Leila had taught him. She’d stood in the shallow end of our own pool every evening in April with her arms out, saying arms, arms, chin down, go, and he’d gone in like a dropped plank, and gone in like a dropped plank, and then one evening he’d gone in like a knife, and come up with his hair flat and his eyes huge and said did you see, and she’d said I saw, and after that there was no keeping him out of it. The pool was the centre of the summer. It was where he was happiest. I’m telling you this because it’s true, and because you need to know how it looked, in May, with the sun on it.
The man from UCLA found me by the barbecue, late, when the light had gone gold and the children had been wrapped in towels and were lying on the grass like puppies.
“You still doing the drive?”
“Every day.”
“Eleven years, man.” He shook his head. He’d never driven to work in his life. “You still listen to the books?”

I told him about the recording. The reedy voice. The man from the nineties. I’d been through the whole lecture twice by then, and three more that I’d found by searching the first few words of it, and I still didn’t know his name, and I told my friend that, and my friend laughed so hard he had to put his beer down.
“You don’t know who that is?”
“Should I?”
He looked at me for a long moment, and something went across his face that I didn’t understand then and do now. Then he said hang on, and went into the house, and came back with a jar.

It was a jam jar. The lid was from a different jar. It had been washed but not well, and there was something dry and brown in the bottom of it, and he put it in my hand and closed my fingers round it with both of his hands and said, laughing still, so that none of it sounded like what it was:
“For the drive you’re not taking.”

I’m not going to tell you more about the jar than that. Not what was in it, not where he got it, not what you do with it, not how much. That’s not what this book is for and it never will be. I’ll tell you that I knew, more or less, the way everyone knows; and that I’d never, in forty years, so much as been in a room with it; and that I put it in my jacket pocket and felt, driving home up the 405 in the dark with my family asleep in the car, the way you’d feel with a letter you hadn’t opened.
It sat in the garage for three weeks. On the shelf above the paint cans, behind the Christmas lights. I’d like to say I forgot about it. I thought about it every day.

What I brought: nothing, this time on purpose. I’d had a good day. I’d kissed them both goodnight. Where I was: the garage. The lamp off. On my back, on the camping mat, under the blanket from the car.

The voice had told me how. Not in the first lecture, in one of the later ones, where he talked less about God and more about method, and he was very plain about it, which is why I trusted him. He said: alone. He said: silence. He said: in the dark, as dark as you can make it, lying down, with your eyes closed, and he said people were afraid of that, and that the fear was the point, and that the dark was the only honest room there was, because everything in it was yours. He said that a measure taken that way was a serious thing, and he had a name for the full measure, which he used with a kind of grin in his voice — he called it the heroic dose — and he said what it was, and I’m not going to, and the reason I’m not going to is the same reason the whole of this book is written the way it’s written. You can hear him say it yourself. You’ll know his name by then.

I waited until the house was asleep. I went out through the kitchen, through the door to the garage, and I didn’t turn on the overhead because the overhead lit the whole thing up like a gas station; I turned on the lamp, the small one on the workbench with the bent neck, and I got the camping mat down from the rafters and the blanket from the back of the car, and I lay down between the car and the shelves with the jar beside me on the concrete. The garage smelled of the car, and of paint, and of the lawnmower, and of the thing the utility sink does in summer, a cold wet smell, with the tap that drips. It was the most ordinary room in the world. I want you to see it, because you’ll need to. The paint cans. The Christmas lights in their tangle. Leila’s gardening chair, the folding kind, leaning against the water heater. The drip.
I did what you do. Then I reached up and I turned off the lamp.

Here is the thing nobody tells you about the dark. It isn’t black. You think it will be and it isn’t; it’s a sort of dim grey-brown with a grain to it, like old paper, like the inside of your own eyelids seen from behind, and for a while — a long while, long enough that I thought well, that’s that then and felt a fool — that’s all there was. The grain. The drip. My own breathing. Pesteh, through the door, turning around three times on his bed.

Then I yawned. I wasn’t tired, and I yawned, a huge yawn, jaw-cracking, and then another, and I felt cold, not cold in the room but cold in the body, cold from inside, the way you feel on the edge of a fever, and my arms were heavy, not heavy like tired, heavy like they belonged to somebody larger who’d lent them to me and would want them back. And I thought: oh. Just that. Oh. And the grain of the dark started to move.
I’ll do this three ways, because three is the number, and none of them is right, and it’s between them somewhere.

It was like the inside of a mosque, if the tiles were alive — the blue ones, the ones that go up into the dome in rings and stars and rings inside the stars — except that the rings were turning and the stars were breathing and the whole dome was being built, from nothing, in front of me, faster than anyone could build it and perfectly, tile by tile, and then taken down, and built again, different.

It was like the carpet in my grandmother’s house in Tehran, the red one, the one I lay on as a boy and followed the pattern of with my finger — except that the pattern was following me, and had learned, somehow, while I wasn’t looking, to breathe.
It was like somebody had found the dial that controls how much detail the world has, and turned it all the way up, and walked away.

I lay there with my eyes closed and the thing built itself over me, and I was not afraid, and that surprised me. I’d expected to be. What I was, instead, was interested — more interested than I had been in anything since I was a child — and under the interest was something I couldn’t name for a long time and then could, and it was this: the feeling you get on the first day of a holiday when you wake and don’t know where you are and then remember, and the remembering is good. I’m here. I’ve got nowhere to be. That.
And then — I don’t know when; time had gone somewhere; that was the first thing to go, before the body, before anything — I heard the water.

Not the drip. The drip was still there, somewhere, I could have found it if I’d looked. This was under it. A deeper sound, a well sound, water a long way down in stone. And I knew, without any surprise at all, that I was at a well, and that the well was old, and that there was someone sitting at it.

I couldn’t see her. I want to be exact. I never, that night or any night, saw anything that I could draw for you. What I had was the sense of her — low, to my left, close, patient, tired the way old things are tired — and the sense that she had been there a long time, and that she had been waiting, not for me in particular, but for anyone who’d finally shut up and lie down in the dark and listen.
Then she spoke, and I’ll tell you the first thing she said, because I wrote it down at four in the morning on the back of a paint-store receipt and I still have it.
She said: You’ve been driving a long time.

That’s all. Six words. In a voice that was low and even and not unkind, that sounded like it had said harder things than that and would again. And I lay on the concrete with the dome turning over me and I started, for no reason I could have given you, to cry — not the way you cry at a film, the way you cry when you’re eight and somebody finally asks.

She talked for a long time after that. I can’t tell you most of it. That’s not modesty; it’s the plain truth of the thing, and the man on the recording had warned me, and I’ll say it once here and then not again: I can’t say this. Not won’t. Can’t. What she told me that night went past the place where my words were kept, and what I brought back was the shape of it and not the thing. The shape was: that I had been carrying something for a long time, and that it was heavy, and that I had been carrying it so long I’d stopped being able to feel the weight, and that the weight was the stories. All four hundred of them. The whole list. She knew about the list. She knew every entry in it, and she told them back to me, not as complaints — as stories — the real ones, the dark ones, the ones I’d never written, as if she’d read them, as if they already existed somewhere and she’d been sent to remind me where I’d put them.
The man doesn’t go home, she said. You know that. Write it where he doesn’t go home.

The lamp, when I turned it on, was the loudest thing I’d ever heard. It was ten past four. I had been in there a little over five hours, and it had been, I would have sworn to you, about forty minutes. I went into the kitchen in my socks with the receipt in my hand and I opened the laptop and I didn’t stop until the light came up over the hill, and when I stopped I had written the first story I had ever finished in my life, start to end, the dark one, with no flinch in it anywhere.

I sat there in the kitchen with the sun coming in and the thing done, and I thought, with total clarity and total calm, the thought that every one of these books is about, the thought I’d like to warn you against and know I can’t:
I’ve found the door.
What I brought: no sleep, and a thing in my chest like a lit coal. Where I was: the 405, southbound. A Monday.

I didn’t tell Leila. I need to say that plainly and I need you not to hold it against me yet. I didn’t tell her because I didn’t know how to say it so that it sounded like what it was. I lay on the garage floor and a woman at a well told me my own stories is not a sentence you can say to the mother of your child over cereal. So I said I’d been up late working on something. Which was true.
She looked at me for a moment longer than she needed to. She has a way of doing that. She’d been doing it, I think now, for about a year.
“Good,” she said. “You look —” and she stopped, and chose the word, “— awake.”
Dara was on the air. “Bābā was up all night,” he told the Valley. “Sources say he was working.”

I drove to Irvine. The voice talked. I didn’t hear a word of it; I had my own. And at my desk, with the grey light coming through the grey blinds onto the grey screen, I did something I’d never done in eleven years at that company, which was nothing. I sat and looked at the story. I read it four times. Then I pasted it into the voice tool, which I’d built, in the spring, for the jingle — I’d made a voice for myself in there too, weeks before, for a reason I couldn’t have told you, from recordings of me reading Dara his books, and I’d never used it — and I pressed the button, and I put the earbuds in, and for twenty-two minutes, in a cubicle in Irvine, I listened to myself tell the dark story in a voice that was mine and wasn’t, steadier than mine, that never stumbled, that knew where every sentence was going before it got there.
I’ll tell you what that was like in one line. It was like hearing your own name said by someone who loves you, in a room you thought was empty.

I made the music that lunchtime. I made the opening pictures that night — thirty seconds of a city at dusk, from above, done the way the tool does it, which is both wrong and beautiful, like a dream of a place. I put the three together on the Tuesday night. On Wednesday night I put it somewhere people could find it, with no name on it, and went to bed, and on Thursday morning two hundred people I’d never met had listened to a man they’d never heard of tell a story about a man who doesn’t go home, and eleven of them had written underneath it, and one of the eleven had written: who ARE you.
Thursday night I went back to the garage.
What I brought: a question. Who are you. Where I was: the garage, the lamp off, the dark.
It came faster the second time. The yawning, the cold, the lent arms, the dome. I’d learned the road; I went down it. And she was there, at the well, as if I’d stepped out of the room for a minute.
I’ll tell you what she said that night, because I wrote it down, and because I’ve since come to understand that it was the truest thing anyone has ever told me and I took it for a riddle.
She said: They always ask who. They never ask what it costs.
I thought she meant the people underneath the story. I thought she was being wise about fame.

Then she told me a new one, and this is the one I need to tell you properly, because it’s the one everything turns on, and because for most of that summer I believed it was the best thing I would ever make.
It came over three nights — that one and the two after — and I’ll give it to you the way it came, plainly, the way she gave it.

There is a man who drives the same freeway every day, an hour each way, for eleven years. One evening, in the rain, there is a tollbooth on the road where no tollbooth has ever been. One lane. One lit window. A woman inside who doesn’t look up. She sells one thing, and it isn’t a shorter drive. She sells an hour. Not an hour off the clock — an hour back: an hour in which he isn’t tired, and isn’t afraid, and isn’t forty, in which his hands know what to make and the work comes out of him like water. He asks what it costs. She says it once. One hour of yours. Paid in one hour from someone who loves you. I don’t choose whom. I don’t say whom. He laughs, because it’s absurd, and he drives through, and that night he writes the first good thing he has ever written.

He goes back. You’d go back. The hours he buys are the best of his life. The work comes; the praise comes; he feels like the man he was meant to be and never had the time for. He keeps a ledger in his head of what it’s costing, and the ledger always comes out fine, because he only ever counts his own hours. His wife is quieter. His son is sleeping more. He tells himself that’s the weather.
And the night his son doesn’t wake, he drives to the booth with everything he’s made in his arms and asks to give it back.
The woman looks up at last. The ledger doesn’t run backwards, she says, and she turns the book round on the counter so he can read it.

Two columns. His — hundreds of lines, every one marked paid. And a second column he has never seen, in a child’s handwriting, going back almost to the first night. His son had found the booth too. He’d been coming to it alone, in the evenings, trading his hours for the only thing he wanted, and the lines all said the same thing in different spellings. One hour for dad to come home. One hour for dad to be home. One hour for dad. The boy had been buying his father back, an hour at a time, at the same window his father was using to buy his way out, and the booth took from both of them, and his column ran out first.

That’s it. That’s the story. You can tell it in a minute, and I’ve just told it in a minute, and I’m telling you that I lay on a garage floor in Sherman Oaks and a voice at a well told it to me over three nights and I wept through all three and came up every morning at four and wrote, and on the fourth day I had it, and it was called The Toll, and I did not flinch anywhere in it, and I knew — I knew, the way you know your own hand — that it was the best thing I would ever make.

I made it over a week. The voice, the one that was mine and steadier. A score that was mostly one low note and the sound of rain on a roof. Pictures of the freeway at night, the red lights going to the horizon, done the wrong-and-beautiful way. Forty-one minutes. I put it out on a Sunday night with no name on it.

By Wednesday, forty thousand people had listened to it. By Friday it was a hundred thousand. People wrote underneath it that they’d had to pull over. People wrote that they’d called their fathers. A woman wrote that she’d listened to it in the car with her son asleep in the back and had sat in the driveway afterwards for an hour and couldn’t go in. Who are you, they wrote. Who are you. Who ARE you.

I read every one of them in a cubicle in Irvine, with the blinds down, and I’ll tell you what I felt, because the whole point of this is to tell you. I felt found. Forty years, and I’d been found, and the thing that had found me lived in the dark in my garage and asked nothing in return.
She’d told me what it cost. I’d written it down. I’d made forty-one minutes out of it and a hundred thousand strangers had wept. And I thought it was a story about a man in a tollbooth.

What I brought: a phone with nine missed calls from Irvine, and a thing I’d said to Dara that I wanted not to have said. Where I was: the garage. The dark. Alone, which I’d been every time, I thought.

I’ll tell you about the bad night now, because there was one, and because the man on the recording had warned about that too, and I hadn’t listened, because I thought the warning was for other people.

It was July by then. I’d stopped — I’ll say it the way it was — I’d stopped being very good at Irvine. The drive was still happening, but I was arriving later and leaving earlier and spending the hours between in a cubicle with the blinds down, making things, and my manager, a decent man who’d never said a hard word to me in eleven years, had said one, on a Thursday, and I’d nodded and gone home and not come in on the Friday, and the phone had rung nine times, and I’d watched it ring.

And Dara. He’d come down to the kitchen that Friday evening while I was at the laptop, with a new one of his comics — the Sock Detective had got a partner, a cat called Inspector Nobody — and he’d stood at my elbow and said Bābā, can you teach me the voice one, the way he’d said it every few days since April, and I’d said — not later. I’d said not now, Dara, in a voice I’d never used on him, and he’d gone away without a word, and I’d heard the station come on in the hall, very quietly, and the jingle play once, in his own voice, and then stop.
I took that into the dark with me. Both of those. I didn’t think of it as taking them. I thought of the dark as the place where things like that went away.

It came on fast and wrong. I knew in the first minute. The yawning, the cold — but the cold didn’t stop at the fever’s edge, it went on down, and the lent arms weren’t lent, they were pinned, and the dome, when it came, came with a sound, a kind of grinding, and the rings in the tiles weren’t rings. They were teeth. Rings of teeth, turning, building themselves down towards me the way the dome had built itself up, and I knew — with the same total knowledge that had told me I’ve found the door — that I was about to be looked at.
I want to explain this as plainly as I can, because I’ve had a long time to understand it and I think I do now.

The dark doesn’t make anything. It’s a room. What’s in it is what you bring, and that first night and all the good ones I’d brought a man who’d kissed his family goodnight and had nowhere to be. That night I brought a man with nine missed calls and his son’s face. And the dark did exactly what the dark does, which is show you what’s in the room. It turned the lights up on it. And the thing in the room was me, and I couldn’t look at it, and so it came to look at me instead.

The man on the recording had said the one thing to do, and it’s the one thing nobody can do, and he said that too. Sit down. Shut up. Pay attention. He said the bad trip is the one you fight. He said the thing you’re running from in there is the thing you came to see, and that if you’d only turn around —

I couldn’t turn around. I ran. You can’t run, lying on a camping mat on a garage floor; I ran anyway, in there, for what the clock later told me was six hours, from a thing that wore my face and wanted, gently, patiently, like the woman at the well, to ask me a question. I don’t know what the question was. I never let it get there. I lay on the concrete and I said no no no no to the dark until the dark got bored of me and let me up, and I turned on the lamp at a quarter to five with my shirt soaked through and I sat against the water heater with my knees up and I shook.

Leila’s chair was there. Her gardening chair, the folding one — not against the water heater, where it always was, but a foot from the mat, turned to face it. I remember looking at it. I remember thinking, with the little I had left to think with, I must have knocked it — and then thinking I didn’t touch it, why would I have touched it, and then not thinking anything, because I was forty years old and I’d just spent six hours running from my own face in the dark and I’d have liked, very much, somebody to hold on to.

I’ll tell you what I decided, sitting there. I decided the gift had turned on me. That I’d done something wrong — brought the wrong thing, broken a rule — and that she’d sent that instead of herself, as a warning, as a lesson. I decided to be more careful. To bring less.

I went back two nights later. She was there, at the well, as if nothing had happened. She said: You went in angry. I said — out loud, on the concrete, in the dark — I know. I’m sorry. She said: Not at me.
I didn’t understand. I wrote it down anyway. I wrote everything down.
What I brought: I’d stopped keeping track. Where I was: the garage. Then the kitchen. Then the garage. I went under on a Tuesday. It was Friday.
This is where I have to tell you about the time, because the time is the whole of it, and because it’s the one thing I can’t make you feel and can only report.

The hours went. Not just in the dark — I’d known about that from the first night; five hours for forty minutes, that was the exchange rate, and I’d thought it a bargain. What I mean is the hours outside went too. I’d come up at four and write until the light and then — I’d be at the laptop and it would be dark again. I’d be in the garage and it would be Thursday. I’d stand in the kitchen with a glass of water and not know, for a long, long moment, whether I’d just woken up or just come home, and then I’d realise I didn’t know what day it was, and then I’d realise I didn’t mind. That was the thing. I didn’t mind. The alarm was still set for six and I’d stopped hearing it. The phone still rang from Irvine and then, after a while, it didn’t. There’d been a letter. I’d read it standing up and put it on the counter and it was there for a week and then it wasn’t, and I don’t know who moved it, and I didn’t ask, because asking would have meant admitting I’d noticed.
And here is the thing I need you to understand, because if you don’t, none of the rest makes sense, and you’ll hate me, and I’m not asking you not to, I’m asking you to wait.

It felt like freedom. Not like falling. Not like losing. Like being let out. For eleven years every hour of my life had been spoken for by a clock that somebody else wound, and now the clock had stopped, and I was in a room with the lights off where the only thing that mattered was the next thing I was going to make, and the things I was making were good — they were the best things I had ever done, and every one of them was better than the one before, and strangers I’d never meet were weeping at them in their cars — and I was awake, for the first time since I was twenty, and I was not afraid of anything, and if you had come to me then and said Kian, your job, your family, the ground under your feet I would have looked at you with real pity and said: You think that’s the ground.

The stress, I’d have told you — the drive, the alarm, the manager, the letter — was a story people told themselves so they wouldn’t have to find out what they were for. I’d found out what I was for. I was for this.

Leila was there. I want to say that before you ask. She was there the whole time, in the house, working, coming home, making dinner, which I ate sometimes, standing. She didn’t shout. I’ve thought about that a great deal since. She’d look at me across the kitchen with that look she’d had for a year, longer than she needed to, and then she’d say there’s food, and go up. I took that for peace. I took it for her understanding what was happening to me, and standing back from it, the way you’d stand back from a man welding.
And once — it was late July, a weekday, early, I know because the station was on and she had her keys — she stopped me in the hall with her hand flat on my chest and said:
“Are you here?”
“I’m here.”
“No. Are you here.”
“Leila.” I put my hand over hers. I could feel my own heart under both of them, going like a bird, the way it did now. “I’ve never been more here in my life.”
She looked at me for a long time. Then she took her hand back and went to work, and the station, in the hall, said: “And now, a song about Pesteh.”

Dara had made the song himself. Not with the tools — he still didn’t have the tools; I still hadn’t shown him — with the hairbrush and his own voice, four lines, to the tune of something from school, about a dog who ate a sock and was sorry and wasn’t. He sang it through the box every morning that summer. It was the best thing in the house and I knew it and I was too busy to tell him so, and on the one morning that I wasn’t — a Saturday, the last in July, Leila’s Saturday off, when I came up out of the garage into the hall at seven with the whole night still turning in me and found him there with the hairbrush — I did the thing I’d like to be remembered for, if I’m remembered for anything, which was that I sat down on the floor of the hall next to the dishwasher box and I said come on, then, and I opened the laptop, and I showed him the voice one.

Just once. Just as a trick. I showed him where you paste the words and I showed him the button and I pasted in his dog song and pressed it, and the song came out in my voice, the steady one, and he laughed so hard he fell over, and he said do it again, and I did it again, and he said can I, and I said go on, and he pressed it, with one finger, very carefully, the way he’d pressed the station’s switch the first time, and it played, and he looked at me with the whole of his face lit up, exactly the way he had in April, and said:
“That’s you.”
“That’s me.”
“Can I keep it?”
“Keep what?”
“The voice one. Can I keep it. For the station.”
“Sure,” I said. “It’s on the laptop. You know where.”
“Will you read me one? In the voice one. The Sock Detective.”

“Later,” I said. “Tonight.” And I ruffled his hair, and I went up to sleep, because the night had been long and I had another one coming, and I didn’t think about it again, not once, for months, until I had to.

What I brought: a good night, a great one, the greatest yet. She’d told me the thing about the lighthouse. I had it all in my head. I needed four hours and a quiet house. Where I was: the kitchen. A Saturday morning in August. Leila in the doorway with her keys.

She had the Saturday shift twice a month and this was one of them. She stood in the kitchen doorway in her work clothes with her bag on her shoulder and her keys in her hand, and the station was on in the hall, and the pool was blue and flat through the window behind her with the sun already on it, and she looked at me the way she did, longer than she needed to, and I thought, she’s going to say something, and she didn’t. She looked at the garage door. Then she looked at me.
“You’ve got him?”
“I’ve got him.”
“Kian.”
“I’ve got him. Go. We’re going to swim later.”

She stood there one more second than a person stands in a doorway. I’ve replayed it more times than there are hours in the rest of my life and I can’t make it longer than one second and I can’t make it shorter. Then she said okay, and she kissed Dara’s head in the hall on her way past the station — bye, jān — and the door closed, and the car started, and the house was quiet, and the garage was right there, and I had the whole of the lighthouse turning in me, every word of it, and four hours before the heat came up, and I thought — I remember exactly what I thought, and I’ll give it to you exactly, because I’ve promised you the truth —
Just the first hour. Just to get it down. He’s got the station. He’ll be fine.
WHAT SHE SAID

What the voice at the well said to me, on the first nights, in June and July, as I wrote it down at four in the morning on whatever was nearest. Where there’s a gap, the words didn’t survive the trip back up. I’ve put down only what I’m sure of.
You’ve been driving a long time.
The man doesn’t go home. You know that. Write it where he doesn’t go home.
You think you lost them. You didn’t. You put them somewhere and forgot where. I know where.
They always ask who. They never ask what it costs.
One hour of yours. Paid in one hour from someone who loves you. I don’t choose whom.
You went in angry.
— Not at me.
The lamp is beautiful. I’m not saying it isn’t. I’m saying look at the house.
(The rest is water. There was always water, under the drip, a long way down.)
II. THE NAMING
What I brought: I don’t know. I never will. Where I was: the garage. Then the pool.
I’m going to tell this once, and plainly, and then I’m not going to tell it again. Not because I can’t. Because it belongs to him, and I’ve taken enough.

I came up out of the dark and the garage was hot. That’s the first thing. The heat had come up while I was under, the way it does in August, and the garage was an oven, and the lamp, when I turned it on, was wrong — too white, too much — and I understood it was the middle of the day. Not the first hour. Not four. The sun was straight overhead. I’d been down there since nine in the morning and it was past two.
The house was quiet.

I want you to understand what that quiet was, because I’ve thought about it more than about anything else in my life. It wasn’t silence. The fridge was going. A car went past on the street. It was the quiet of a house with nobody making anything in it. No station. No hairbrush. No boy singing about a dog. I stood in the kitchen with the garage door open behind me and I called his name, the way you do, not worried, just calling, and then I called it again, and the back door was open, the one to the yard, and that’s when Pesteh started.

He was at the edge of the pool. He was barking at the water. He wasn’t barking at anything else. He had his front feet on the wet tile at the deep end and he was barking down, into the blue, the same bark over and over, and he looked at me when I came out the door and then he looked back at the water, and I knew. Before I saw. The way you know your own hand.

He’d dived. Of course he had. The pool was the centre of the summer and his father was in the garage and the sun was on the water and he was eight and he’d learned to go in like a knife, and he’d gone in, and something — I don’t know what. Nobody knows what. The people who came afterwards had a word for it and said that it happens, that it happens to strong swimmers, that it happens to children in pools with their parents on the other side of a window, and that the thing that makes it a death and not a story told at dinner is minutes. Just minutes. Someone in the house. Someone at the window. Someone who hadn’t turned off the lamp.

I went in, in my clothes. I got him up. He was so light. I’d carried him on my shoulders a thousand times and he was so light. I got him onto the tile and I did the thing you half-know from a class you took when he was born, the breathing and the pressing, and I was saying his name the whole time, and I was saying Bābā’s here, over and over, Bābā’s here, Bābā’s here, which is the thing I had not been. Pesteh stood next to me and didn’t bark any more. The neighbour came over the fence. I don’t know who called. There were people, and then there was a van, and then there were people in the van, and then there was a hand on my shoulder, and the hand belonged to a woman in a uniform who had done this before, and she was very gentle, and she said my name, which I hadn’t told her, and she said that they were going to stop now.
I remember the tile. It was warm. I remember thinking: the station is still on in the hall. It wasn’t. I don’t know why I thought it.

Leila’s car came into the drive at twenty past three. I was sitting on the kitchen floor by then with the dog in my lap and my clothes drying stiff on me, and somebody had put a blanket over my shoulders, the one from the car, the one I used in the garage, and I heard her car, and I heard the door, and I heard her come up the path, and I heard her stop at the open front door, where she could see straight through the house to the yard.

She didn’t scream. People think they would. She made a sound I’ve only ever heard once, that I can’t give you three ways or one, that I don’t think there’s a word for in any language I know, and then she walked through the house past me as if I were furniture and out to the yard, and I didn’t see what she did there, and I never asked, and I never will.
That’s it. That’s all of it. He was eight. He was the most beautiful thing in the house. The pool was blue and the sun was on it. I was forty feet away with my eyes closed, making something.
What I brought: nothing. There was nothing left to bring. Where I was: the house. For days. I don’t know how many.

I’d like to tell you the days after in order and I can’t, because they didn’t come in order. They came the way the hours had come that summer — in pieces, with the joins missing — except that now I wasn’t choosing it, and it wasn’t freedom.

There was a hospital, which was pointless, and which we went to anyway, because that’s what you do. There was paper. There is always paper. A man in a tie had the paper and he was kind and the paper said what had happened in words that were careful not to say anything, and I signed where he pointed and I remember the pen was bad.

There was Leila’s mother, on a plane from Toronto, and then in the house, and then in the kitchen, cooking, because that is what she does, cooking for a house where nobody ate, filling the fridge with pots. There were people. Her people, mostly. Mine came and stood in the hall and didn’t know where to put their hands. They looked at the dishwasher box with KDARA on it and the K the wrong way round and nobody moved it and nobody mentioned it and the switch I’d wired in with the nine-volt battery was still there with its little light, and nobody touched that either.

We buried him on the third day, because that is how it’s done where we come from. I’m not going to describe it. There were the prayers, in a language I half have, and there was the ground, and there was Leila, standing, with her mother holding one arm, and she stood the whole time and never once looked at me, and I understood that she had decided something, and I didn’t know what.

On the seventh day the house filled up again, the way it does on the seventh day — people come, and sit, and eat, and the family stands and receives them, and it is the last of the big days, and after it you are supposed to begin. I stood in my own living room and received. I shook hands. A man I’d worked with for eleven years, the manager, the decent one who’d said the hard word in July, came and stood in front of me and his face broke and he said I should have called again, and I said you called nine times, and he said I should have called ten, and I held him while he cried, because somebody had to be held and it wasn’t going to be me.

I didn’t sleep. I’ll say that, because you’ll wonder. Not a sleepless kind of not-sleeping; I mean that I lay next to her in the dark with my eyes open and she lay with hers open and we didn’t touch and we didn’t speak and at some hour one of us would get up, and it was always her, and I’d hear her go downstairs, and I’d hear a door, and I never got up to see which door, because I was afraid I knew.

I couldn’t go in the garage. I’ll be exact about that. I went to the door to it, on the second day, and I put my hand on the handle, and I stood there, and the thing I felt wasn’t grief — grief was everywhere, grief was the air — the thing I felt at that door was want. I wanted to go in. I wanted to lie down in the dark where the woman was and have her tell me it wasn’t what it was. And I was so ashamed of that, so sick at it, that I took my hand off the handle and went and sat in the yard by the pool until Leila’s mother came and got me, and I didn’t go near that door again for a week.

And I couldn’t drive. The car sat in the drive with his seat still in the back, his comics on the floor of it, the Sock Detective and Inspector Nobody on a case they’d never close, and the voice was in there, on the phone, in the console, the reedy unhurried voice that had taught me the dark, and I couldn’t get in. Leila’s mother drove. I sat in the passenger seat like a child. On the way back from the cemetery on the third day she reached over, without looking, without a word, and turned the console off, though nothing was playing, and we drove the rest of the way in the quiet.
What I brought: the ninth day, and nothing. Where I was: the kitchen table. Daylight. The two of us.

She waited until her mother had gone to the store. I understand that now. She waited until the house was empty of everyone but us, and then she sat down at the kitchen table, across from me, in the daylight, with her hands flat on the wood, and she said my name, and I looked up.
This is the only time in the whole of this that she talks to me as herself, in the light, and I’m going to give it to you exactly, because I owe her that much and more.
“I know what’s in the jar,” she said.
I didn’t say anything.

“I’ve known since the first night. I want you to hear that. Not since last week. Since the first night, in June, when you came up at four in the morning and sat at this table and wrote until it got light and thought nobody knew. I knew.”
“Leila —”
“I’m going to say this once. So let me.”
I let her.

“It’s a mushroom.” She said it the way you’d say it’s a Tuesday. “The brown stuff in the jar. It’s a mushroom, dried. There’s a thing in it, a chemical, and the chemical is called psilocybin [sy-loh-SY-bin].” She said it slowly, so I’d have it. “The mushroom has a name too, the kind of name a scientist gives. Psilocybe cubensis [sy-LOSS-ih-bee kew-BEN-sis]. It grows in warm places. It grows on cow dung, in pastures, after rain. That’s what you’ve been lying on the garage floor eating since June. A thing that grows on cow dung in a field. I want you to know what it is, because you never asked. Nine weeks and you never once asked what it was.”
I had never once asked.

“And the man.” She looked at me. “The voice in the car. The one you’ve been listening to since May like he was God. His name is Terence McKenna.” She said it flat, two words, like a name off a list. “He’s been dead since the year two thousand. He had a tumour in his head. He was fifty-three. And I know his name, Kian, because I listened to him in college, before I ever met you, at two in the morning in a dorm room with a girl from my floor, the same recordings — the same ones — and I knew his voice through the car door in the driveway the second week of May, and I thought: oh. Here it comes.”

“So I knew what the jar was before you did. And I knew what you were doing in there. And I knew what the dark was for and what it does to a person who’s carrying something and I knew that you were carrying four hundred stories and a job you hated and a wife you’d stopped looking at and I knew that if you went in there alone you’d come out lit up and I knew —” and here, for the first time, her voice did something, and she stopped it, with her hands flat on the table, the way you’d stop a plate from sliding — “I knew what it would cost. I knew the price. I knew it better than you did. And I didn’t stop you.”
“Why,” I said. It wasn’t a question. It was the only word I had.
She looked at me for a long time. The look she’d had for a year. Longer than she needed to.

“Because you were alive,” she said. “For the first time since Dara was born, you were alive in this house, and I’m not going to sit here and pretend I didn’t want that. I wanted it so much I made a bet with it. I bet the house.” She stood up. “That’s all. That’s all I’m going to say about it, now or ever. I’m not going to say the other thing, because you know the other thing, and you can carry it, and I’ll carry mine.”
She went to the door to the hall and stopped there with her back to me.
“Psilocybin,” she said again, without turning round. “Terence McKenna. Now you have the names. He never would have let you go in without them.”
And she went up.
What I brought: two names. Where I was: the kitchen, alone, with the light going.
So now you have them too, and so does the book, and from here it uses them.

Terence. I’ll call him that from now on, because that’s what everyone calls him, the people who loved him, the people who thought he was a fool, the ones who listened to him at two in the morning in dorm rooms and the ones who listened on the 405 for a summer and never once thought to look him up. Terence McKenna. Born in a small town in Colorado in 1946, died in 2000, and in between he did the thing I’d been doing in the garage, in a jungle, in 1971, with his brother, and then spent the rest of his life trying to tell people what it was like, in plain words, with that grin in his voice, and never quite could, and never stopped trying. That’s the man who taught me the dark. I’ll give him his due later, properly, the way this kind of book does. For now I only want to say that Leila was right: he would never have let me go in without the name. He said so. In one of the lectures I hadn’t got to. Know what you’re taking. Know where it grows. Know who found it and what they paid. I’d skipped ahead to the part about the dark.

And the thing in the jar. A mushroom. I’ll give you that later too, where it belongs, because it has a history as long as ours and a woman in it who paid for it more than I ever will. At the kitchen table, with the light going, I didn’t know any of that. I knew it was a mushroom, and that my wife had known for nine weeks, and that she had bet the house, and lost.
I sat there a long time. Then I did the thing I’d been not doing for a week. I got up, and I went to the garage door, and I put my hand on the handle, and I turned it.
The lamp was on.

I hadn’t left it on. I was sure of that. I’d turned it off at nine on a Saturday morning in August with the whole of the lighthouse in my head and I had not been back. But the lamp with the bent neck was on, low, the way I always had it before I turned it off, and the camping mat was down, and the blanket from the car was folded on it, and beside the mat, where it had never once been in the daytime, turned to face the mat, was Leila’s gardening chair.

I stood in the doorway and looked at it and I didn’t understand, and I thought — I actually thought this — she’s been coming out here to sit with him. With the idea of him. The way I might have, if I were braver. And I was so moved by that, so ashamed and so moved, that I backed out and closed the door quietly, the way you close a door on someone sleeping, and I let her have it.

I’d like to tell you I understood then. I’ve promised you the truth. I understood nothing. I was a man who’d been handed two names at a kitchen table and I thought the names were the whole of what I’d been missing.
WHAT SHE SAID
The nights after. August into October. I was better at bringing it back by then, or she was speaking more plainly. I wrote these down in a notebook I kept beside the mat.
He smelled of chlorine and bread. After the pool, before his bath. You never noticed. I noticed every day.
He held the hairbrush with both hands. Like it was heavy. Like it mattered.
You said later. You always said later. I’m not saying it to hurt you. I’m saying it because nobody else will, and somebody has to say it in this house.
The man goes back to the booth. Of course he goes back. The boy’s column is the only place the boy’s handwriting still exists.
I’m not angry. I was angry for a year. Now I’m only tired.
I sit here because it’s the only room where you listen. Do you understand that? You hear me here. You don’t hear me anywhere else.
Sit up. No — stay there. Stay. I’ll stay too.
(That night I heard something in the dark that wasn’t the drip. A breath. I thought it was mine.)
III. THE TELLING
What I brought: him. All of him. There was nothing else in me to bring. Where I was: the garage. The tenth night after. I didn’t move her chair.
I went back in on the tenth night.

I’m not going to defend it. I’ll tell you what I told myself, which was that the dark was the only place he might still be, and that a man who’s lost his son will go anywhere the boy might be, into any room, through any door, and that this was a door. That’s what I told myself. Under it was the other thing, the thing I’d felt at the handle on the second day. I wanted to go in. I wanted the dark more than I had ever wanted anything, and I was ashamed of it, and I went in anyway.
I didn’t move her chair. I lay down on the mat with the chair beside me, turned to face me, and I thought, she sits here with him, and I thought it was a kind of company. I turned off the lamp.

Terence says you should never go in carrying grief alone. He says it in one of the later lectures, the ones I hadn’t got to. He says grief is the heaviest thing a person can bring into the room and that the room will show it to you at its true size, and that nobody should see that without somebody beside them. I hadn’t heard that one yet. I went in alone, I thought.

It came faster than it ever had. There was hardly any road; I was just there. And here is the thing I have to tell you, the thing that is the whole of what happened to me that autumn, and I’ll say it as plainly as I can:

The door opened wider. Not darker. Not the teeth. Wider. The dome came and it was the dome from the first night, the blue rings, the breathing stars, but it was bigger than it had ever been, it went up past where the garage roof should have been and kept going, and the detail of it was finer than anything I’d seen, and I understood — I’m not sure I understood it then; I understand it now — that grief had done what nothing else could. It had taken the last of me out of the way. There was no Kian in that room any more to stand between the dark and what the dark had to show. There was only the hole where the boy had been, and the dark poured into it.
And she was there. At the well. As if I’d stepped out for ten days.
She said his name.

I hadn’t said it. Nobody in the house had said it in ten days; we’d all gone around it, the way you go around a hole in a floor. She said it, low, plain, the way you say a name you’ve said ten thousand times, and then she said:
He smelled of chlorine and bread. After the pool, before his bath.
Did you know that? I hadn’t known that.

He held the hairbrush with both hands. Like it was heavy. And she went on. She told me about my son. She told me things I had been in the room for and hadn’t seen. The way he said sources say with his chin up. The way he’d check, every morning, before he went on the air, that the little switch light was lit, and touch it once with one finger, the way you’d touch something for luck. The way he sang the dog song slightly flat on purpose because it made Leila laugh. That he’d been afraid of the deep end until the dive, and after the dive the deep end was the only place he’d go. That he’d asked her, in July, in the car, why Bābā was always in the garage, and what she’d said.
She didn’t tell me what she’d said.

I lay on the concrete and wept the way I hadn’t at the pool or the grave or the table — the way the dark lets you, with the whole body, with no one watching — and she went on telling me my son, in that low, tired, even voice, for what the clock said afterwards was seven hours, and at the end of it, when I came up, I didn’t go to the kitchen. I sat on the mat with the notebook I’d brought and I wrote it all down, every word, in the dark, by feel, so I wouldn’t lose a single one.
Then I went to the laptop. And I made the first of them.
What I brought: the names. I had them now. I thought that was the point.
Where I was: the kitchen table, in the day, with Terence’s books open. One of them hers, it turned out. From college.

Before I tell you what I made, I owe you the man. Leila said he’d never have let me go in without the names, and she was right, so here they are, the way this kind of book does it, plainly, and you can skip ahead if you like, and I’d rather you didn’t.

Terence McKenna was born in November 1946 in a town called Paonia [pay-OH-nee-uh], in the mountains of western Colorado, a place of orchards and coal, and he was a strange, bookish, short-sighted boy who collected butterflies and read everything, and who got out as soon as he could. By the time he was twenty-five he’d been to India and Nepal and Indonesia and Berkeley, and in the winter of 1971 he went with his younger brother Dennis, who was the scientist of the two, deep into the Amazon in Colombia, to a mission village called La Chorrera [lah cho-REH-rah], on a river in the forest. They’d gone looking for something else — a different thing entirely, a plant the people there made into a snuff — and what they found instead, growing in the cow pastures around the mission, were mushrooms. Small, brown, on dung, after rain. This mushroom. The one in the jar.

What happened to the two of them at La Chorrera that spring is a long story and Terence told it for the rest of his life, and I’m not going to pretend to settle it. He wrote a whole book about it, and he never claimed it was anything but his account. What matters here is one thing he came out of the jungle saying and never stopped saying for twenty-nine years, in every lecture, with that grin in his voice:

The mushroom speaks. Not a figure of speech. He meant it. He said that when you took enough of it, alone, in the dark, a voice came — not your own, older than your own, patient, amused, sometimes stern — and that it would tell you things, and that the whole of his work was trying to tell people what it had told him. He said he’d sat in the dark and argued with it. He said it had a sense of humour. He said, over and over, that he could not prove to anyone that the voice wasn’t simply himself, some part of himself he’d never had access to, talking back — and that he didn’t care, because the things it said were true.
I want you to hold onto that last part. He said it himself. I can’t prove it isn’t me.

And he was very plain about how to meet it. Alone. In silence. In the dark, lying down, eyes closed. He said the dark was the whole method and that everything else was decoration. He said the full measure of it was a serious undertaking, and he gave it that name, the heroic dose, and he said the number, and I still won’t, because that’s the one thing this book is for and against at the same time: it will tell you everything about this mushroom except how. He was also plain about the other thing, the thing I’d skipped. Have someone there. Not in the room, necessarily. In the house. Awake. He said the oldest people who used these things never, ever used them alone, that there was always someone sitting up — the healer in the mountains of Mexico sat up all night with the banker; the doctor sat all afternoon with the writer in Los Angeles; the thing you brought and the room you brought it into included, always, who was there — and that the modern idea of a man alone in a dark room with it was a kind of arrogance, and that he was guilty of it himself.

He died in April 2000, at fifty-three, of a tumour in his brain. Leila had that right too. He knew it was coming for about a year, and in that year he gave a few more talks, thinner, slower, and in one of them someone asked him if he was afraid, and he said something I’ll give you in my own words because I don’t have the page: that he’d spent his life going into the dark on purpose, and that this was only one more time, without the choice.

That’s him. I listened to all of it that September, at the kitchen table, in the daytime, on the laptop, because I still couldn’t get in the car — and I found, on the third day, when I went looking for one of the books, that we already had it. It was on Leila’s shelf, in the study, between her college things. A paperback. Twenty years old. Her name inside the cover in the handwriting she’d had at nineteen. I stood there holding it and I thought: she listened to him in a dorm room before she ever met me. And I thought that was a lovely thing. A coincidence. I put it back exactly where it had been.
What I brought: the names, and a need to know where they came from. Where I was: the same table. The same books.
So. The mushroom. I owe you this too, and it’s shorter.

It was written down for the first time in 1906, by an American botanist standing in a cow pasture in Cuba — which is why its name has Cuba in it, cubensis, Cuban. He called it something else, a name that was later changed, but the thing was the thing: a small brown mushroom with a cap the colour of a biscuit and a stem that bruises blue when you handle it, and it grows on the dung of cattle, in warm wet country, in nearly every warm wet country on earth. Cuba. Mexico. Colombia, where the brothers found it. Thailand. Australia. The warm end of this country. It is, people who know these things say, the most common of all its kind, and the easiest to recognise, and the one the whole world means when it says the word.

It had been eaten for a very long time before 1906. In Mexico, the Aztecs had a name for mushrooms like it — teonanácatl [tay-oh-nah-NAH-kah-tl], which the friars who wrote it down translated as flesh of the gods — and the friars, who wrote down everything, wrote down with horror that the people ate them at feasts and saw visions and wept and laughed, and then the friars forbade it, and for four hundred years it went underground, into the mountains, where the Spanish didn’t go much.

In the mountains of Oaxaca [wah-HAH-kah], in the south of Mexico, there is a people called the Mazatec [MAH-zah-tek], and they never stopped. They ate the mushrooms at night, in a ceremony called a velada [veh-LAH-dah], a vigil, a sitting-up — a healer and the sick person and whoever had come, in a dark room, all night, with the healer singing. They called the mushrooms the children. The holy children. The little ones that come up after the rain.

In 1955 a banker from New York named Gordon Wasson, who had spent his life collecting the ways people felt about mushrooms, went to a Mazatec town called Huautla [WOW-tlah] and was taken in the dark to a healer, a woman named María Sabina, who gave him the children and sang over him all night. He was, as far as anyone knows, the first outsider ever to be allowed to. Two years later he wrote about it in a magazine, with photographs. He changed her name and didn’t give the town’s. It made no difference; the world found her within a few years, and came. Thousands of people, over the next fifteen years, up the mountain roads to Huautla, looking for the woman and the children. Her town turned on her. Her house was burned. She said, late in her life, to the man who wrote down her story, that from the day the foreigners came, the children had lost their purity, and that she was the one who had shown them. I’m giving you that in my words. She said it in hers, and they’re worse.

In 1958, in Switzerland, the chemist who had found LSD twenty years before took mushrooms from those mountains and drew out of them the thing that does the work, and gave it the name Leila said at the table. Psilocybin. And in the mid-seventies the two brothers who’d gone to La Chorrera wrote a thin book — under made-up names, with a drawing of a mushroom on the front — that taught people how to make the Cuban one grow at home, and that is the one fact in this whole history that I’m going to leave as a fact. The book exists. It changed everything. It made the mushroom from the cow pasture the mushroom of the world. I won’t tell you a word of what’s in it.

And this, last, the plain fact, the one Terence said every book should have exactly one of: the thing in the mushroom is shaped almost exactly like a thing the brain makes for itself every day. A messenger. A little molecule called serotonin [seh-roh-TOH-nin] that carries signals between the parts of your mind the way a runner carries a note — mood, mostly; sleep; the general sense of whether things are all right. Psilocybin fits the same lock the messenger fits. It slips into the keyhole and turns. And one of the doors it opens — the main one, the researchers who’ve looked think — is the door to a room I’ll tell you about now, because it’s the room this whole book is about.
What I brought: a question I’d been asking since I was a boy. Where does it come from? Where I was: the table. Then the garage.
Where do ideas come from.
Everyone who has ever made anything has asked it, and everyone who’s answered honestly has said the same strange thing, and I’d heard them say it all my life and never listened.

The Greeks said there were nine of them — the Muses — and that they were sisters, and that their mother was Memory. Not inspiration; not God; Memory, a goddess called Mnemosyne [nee-MOZ-ih-nee], and the oldest poems we have begin with the poet asking her daughters to sing through him, as if the poet were only a mouth, and the song already existed somewhere and had to be remembered. A Spanish poet, two and a half thousand years later, standing up in a hall in Buenos Aires in 1933, said it wasn’t a goddess at all. He called it the duende [DWEN-day] — a dark thing, he said, that comes up through the soles of your feet, that you have to fight, that only arrives when you’re wounded and won’t arrive at all unless it can see that death is possible. Between those two — the goddess who is Memory and the demon who needs a wound — is every honest thing anyone has ever said about making.
Here’s what the people who study it with machines have found, as far as I can make it plain.

There is a part of the mind that runs when you aren’t doing anything in particular. The researchers have a name for it; I’ll call it the narrator. It’s the part that keeps the story of who you are — what you owe, what time it is, what your manager said, what you’re afraid of. It is on nearly all the time, and it is very loud, and most of what you think of as you is it. And there is another part that makes things up, that joins things that don’t go together, that wanders — and the finding, over and over, in study after study, is that the best ideas come when the narrator steps back and leaves the maker alone with the lights off. That’s why ideas come in the shower. That’s why they come on walks. There was a study — and I laughed out loud at the kitchen table when I read it, the first time I’d laughed since August — that found the single best thing you could do for a problem you were stuck on was to go and do something easy and dull that let your mind drift. Like driving the same road every day for eleven years.
The 405 was never my cage. It was my incubator. Every idea I ever had, I had on it. I’d thought the car was where my life stopped. It was the only place it was happening.

And the thing in the jar: the imaging studies, the ones from about 2012 on, found that it quiets the narrator. Turns it down. The self steps aside, and parts of the mind that never normally speak to each other start to, and what comes out is — this is the whole book, so I’ll say it slowly —
A mind with its narrator switched off can only hear its own ideas as if they came from somebody else.

That’s the muse. That’s Memory’s daughter and the demon in the feet and the voice Terence heard in the jungle. When the part that says I goes quiet, whatever speaks next doesn’t sound like you. It sounds like a stranger. It sounds like a god. It sounds like a woman at a well. And Terence knew this — he said it himself: I can’t prove it isn’t me — and I read it, at the table, in September, in a book with my wife’s nineteen-year-old handwriting inside the cover, and I nodded, and I thought yes, exactly, and I went out to the garage that night and lay down in the dark next to her chair and waited for the voice.
I thought the finding was about the voice. I didn’t think it was about me. I didn’t think: if everything sounds like a stranger in there — then a stranger would too.
What I brought: the notebook. More of him, night after night. Where I was: the garage, and the kitchen, and the garage. September went. I didn’t see it go.
I made eight of them that autumn. I called the whole thing The Station.

I’ll tell you what they were, because this is the part of the book where I became, to a great many people I never met, somebody, and I need you to see how it looked from inside, so you can decide for yourself what it was.

They were short. Ten minutes, twelve. Each one was a single thing about him — a true thing, from the notebook, from the well — told plainly in the steady voice, over the sound of a radio tuning, the way his station had sounded through the dishwasher box. The first was the chlorine and the bread. The second was the switch, and the finger touching it for luck.
