The third was the dive — the whole spring of it, Leila in the shallow end with her arms out saying chin down, go, and the plank, and the plank, and the knife. The fourth was the hairbrush, held with both hands. The fifth was the dog song, slightly flat on purpose. I didn’t use his voice. That’s true, and I’d like it known. I had it, in the laptop, from the jingle, and I never once used it. I used mine.

They were the best things I’ve ever made and they are the best things I will ever make and I knew it as I made them. I’d come up out of the dark at four with the notebook full of him and I’d sit at the table and the thing would come out whole, in an hour, the way The Toll had, and it would be right — every word where it should be, nothing to fix — and I’d put it out before the sun was up and go and lie down and not sleep.

And the world came. The hundred thousand from the summer were waiting, and they came, and they brought others. By October a number I won’t write down had listened to a man they didn’t know tell them, in ten-minute pieces, about a boy they would never meet, and they wrote underneath it the kind of things people write, and some of them were from people who had lost children and some of them were from people who were afraid to, and a woman wrote that she’d gone upstairs after the dive one and lain down on the floor of her daughter’s room and the daughter had asked what was wrong and she hadn’t been able to say. Who are you, they wrote, still. And then they found out. Somebody put it together — the voice from The Toll — and then there were people who wanted to talk to me, real ones, with companies, and the thing I’d made by myself in a dark garage out of my dead son was going to be, if I wanted, a thing with a budget and a building and a parking lot.

I didn’t want. Let me be clear about that. I didn’t do it for them, and I didn’t answer the companies, and I didn’t take the money, and when a newspaper wrote about The Station I didn’t read it. I did it because the garage was the only place on earth where he was still alive, and the laptop was the only way to bring him up out of it into the light, and if I stopped, he’d stop.

That is the truth and here is the other truth, and they sit side by side and I can’t make them agree. I was making art out of my son. The best art of my life. Strangers wept at it. And I knew — not later; then, every morning at four with the notebook open — that the thing I was feeling, under the grief, in the hour when it came out whole and right, was joy.

Leila watched. She was there. She went to work and came home and made food that I sometimes ate and she stood in the kitchen doorway some nights while I was at the laptop and watched me, with the look, longer than she needed to, and she didn’t say a word about The Station, not one, though she must have known, the whole city knew. She said there’s food, and went up. And later I’d hear her come down. And the door.
What I brought: the second half. Where I was: the garage. The chair beside me, where it always was now.

She told me the rest of The Toll on a night in October, and I’m going to give it to you the way she gave it, plainly, because the first half was the best thing I ever made and the second half is the truest, and they are the same story.
The man goes back to the booth.

Of course he goes back. The night after the funeral he drives the freeway in the rain and there’s the one lit window, and the woman doesn’t look up, and he stops. He doesn’t ask for an hour. He asks to see the ledger. She turns it round. And he reads the boy’s column — one hour for dad to come home, in the child’s hand, in the different spellings — and he reads it from the first line to the last, and then he reads it again.

He asks her for an hour. She tells him the price, the same as always: paid by someone who loves you. He says there’s nobody left. She says there’s one. He says take it, and drives through, and that night, in the hour she gave him, he makes the most beautiful thing he has ever made, and it’s about the boy, and people stand in the road and weep at it.

He goes back every night. He knows now what the hours are made of. He knows whose column they come from — the only column left, the one with his wife’s name at the top — and he reads the boy’s handwriting every night before he pays, because the ledger is the only place on earth where the boy’s handwriting still exists, and then he pays, and drives through, and makes the beautiful thing.

The last time, the woman looks up. She’s nearly out, she says. He says: I know. She says: And then? He says: Then I’ll have made everything there is to make of him, and it will all be beautiful, and I’ll be done. And she turns the book round so he can see his wife’s column, and it is almost empty, and the last few lines in it are not in his wife’s hand. They’re in the child’s. Written before. Saved up. One hour for dad, in case.

That’s the end of The Toll. She told it to me in the dark and I lay there and didn’t weep, for once; I lay there and understood that I’d been handed the darkest story I had ever heard and that it was finished and perfect and that I was going to make it, and I came up at four and made it in a day, and it was the ninth piece, and I put it out with the other eight, and it was, people said, the best of them. A man letting the last of his family pay for his art and calling it love. People wrote that they couldn’t breathe.

I made it. I put it out. I didn’t once think it was about me. I’ve promised you the truth and that is the truth: I had the narrator switched off, every night, by choice, and the thing you can’t hear with the narrator off is your own name.
What I brought: nothing — I thought. But you can’t bring nothing. I know that now. Where I was: the garage. The lamp off. The chair.
There was one more bad night. I’ll tell it short.

It was late October. I’d made the ninth piece. I went in light — I thought — I went in the way I had in June, interested, nowhere to be, and it came on wrong anyway. The cold that didn’t stop. The pinned arms. The teeth.

But I was different by then. I’d been in the dark forty nights since August and I had read the books and I had heard Terence say it again, in his thin voice in the last year of his life — the thing you’re running from in there is the thing you came to see — and when the face came, the one that wore mine, patient, asking, I didn’t run.

I turned around. In there. I don’t know how else to say it. I stopped, and I turned, and I let it come, and it came, and it looked at me, and it asked its question, and the question was the one I’d been running from since July.

Where were you? And I answered it. Out loud, on the concrete, in the dark, with my voice cracking. I was in here. I was forty feet away with my eyes closed. I was making something. And the teeth stopped turning. Just stopped. The dome went still and then it went soft and then it was the blue rings again, breathing, the first night’s dome, and the thing that had worn my face wasn’t anything, it was just the dark, and I lay there shaking and I thought: that’s all it wanted. It wanted me to say it.
And in the quiet after, in the dark, I heard something that wasn’t the drip.

A breath. Not mine — mine was ragged; this was held, and then let go, carefully, the way you breathe when you’re trying not to make a sound. Close. To my left. And the creak of something — canvas, a joint — the sound a folding chair makes when somebody in it shifts their weight.

I lay very still. And I thought — I give you this exactly — I thought: she’s here with him. I thought the room had let her in. I thought the dark had opened wide enough that she had come to the well too, from wherever she was, and was sitting in her chair in the vision with me, and that this was the kindest thing it had ever done.
I said, into the dark: I’m sorry.
And the voice at the well — low, tired, close, the voice that had told me every story I’d ever made — said: I know.
What I brought: November. Where I was: the house. It was dark earlier now. I hadn’t changed the bulbs.

The house went dark that autumn, and I mean it plainly. The bulb in the hall went in October and I didn’t change it. The one over the stove went. The porch light. I’d come up out of the garage at four and go through the house to the laptop in the dark, by feel, and I liked it; the dark was where I lived now, and the kitchen was only the part of the garage with a table in it. Leila changed the ones she could reach. She didn’t say anything about it. She did say, once, standing at the top of the stairs in the dark, in her coat, going to work:
“Are you here?”
I was at the bottom of the stairs with the notebook. I looked up at her.
“I’m with him,” I said.
She stood there a long moment. Then she went out, and the door closed, and I heard her car, and I went to the garage.

She’d gone thin. I saw that. I want it on the record that I saw it — I’m not going to pretend I was blind; I was something worse than blind, I was looking at the wrong thing — that she’d gone thin, that her mother had gone back to Toronto in October and the pots had stopped, that she came home later than she used to and went up earlier, that the dishwasher box was still in the hall with KDARA on it and the switch light had finally gone out, the battery dead, and nobody had changed that either.

And the nights were changing. She came less — the voice at the well, I mean. I’d go down, and lie in the dark, and the dome would come, as big as ever — bigger, the door had never been wider — and I’d wait at the well, and she wouldn’t be there. Some nights. Then most. Then I’d lie there for six hours in the most beautiful dark I’d ever been in with nothing in it but the drip, and I’d come up with the notebook empty, and I’d think: I’ve used it up. I’ve asked too much. Every story has a bottom and I’ve reached it. Terence had said that too, that the voice could withdraw, that it wasn’t yours and it could go. I thought that’s what was happening. I thought the gods were taking it back.

The last night she came was the fourteenth of November. I know because I wrote it in the notebook. She said very little. She said, You said later. She said, I’m only tired. And she said one thing I didn’t write down, because I didn’t understand it, and I’ll put it here in the plain words she used, which I only remembered after, when I had the recording:
I’m going to stop coming, Kian. Not because I don’t love you. Because I can’t sit in the dark any more and watch you not know who I am.

I thought it was the god, saying goodbye. I lay there and wept and said thank you, over and over. Thank you for everything you gave me. And the chair creaked, and the breath went out, carefully, and I heard — I can tell you now what I heard, because I know — I heard a woman get up out of a folding chair in a dark garage and stand for a moment looking down at her husband on the floor, and then go in through the kitchen door, quietly, the way you close a door on someone sleeping.
She didn’t come again. Not to the well. And on the nineteenth of November, I came up out of the dark at four in the morning, and went through the house by feel, and the house was empty.
WHAT SHE SAID
The first night — the whole of it this time, from a file recorded on a phone, not from my notes. It begins with the timestamp the phone gave it.

IV. THE ROOM
What I brought: nothing. I came up empty. The well had been dry for five nights. Where I was: the house. Four in the morning. The nineteenth of November. Empty.
I knew before I’d crossed the kitchen.

You know a house. You know it the way you know a body — by its sounds, by the weight of the air in it. The fridge was going. A car went past. And under that, where there should have been the sound of a sleeping woman a floor up, a sound you can’t hear and can, there was nothing. I stood in the dark kitchen with the notebook in my hand, empty, and I said her name, the way I’d said his on a Saturday in August, not worried, just calling, and the house gave it back to me.

I went up by feel. Our room. The bed made. Her side of the closet open and the hangers bare, the way hangers look when they’ve been emptied quickly and all at once. Her books gone from the study — the shelf where the paperback had been, the one with her nineteen-year-old handwriting inside, was a gap with dust on either side of it. Dara’s room I didn’t go into. I stood at the door. The dishwasher box was in the hall where it had always been, with KDARA on it and the K the wrong way round, and the dead switch, and the hairbrush was gone from the hole in the front. She’d taken the hairbrush. She’d left me the box.

No note. I looked. I looked the way you look, in the places people leave notes — the table, the counter, the pillow, the fridge under a magnet — and there wasn’t one, and I understood that this was itself the note. She had said it all once, at the table, in the daylight, and she had told me she wouldn’t say it again, and she was a woman who did what she said.

Then I came back down into the kitchen, and the laptop was open on the table, which it always was, and the screen was lit, which it never was at that hour, and on it was a folder I had never made, and the folder was called Garage.
What I brought: I sat down. Where I was: the kitchen table. The laptop. The lamp in the garage still on behind me through the open door.

Sixty-one files. Recordings, made on a phone and copied over, each one with a date and a time. The first one was the fifteenth of June, a little before one in the morning. The last was the fourteenth of November. I looked at the two dates for a long time and I didn’t open anything, because some part of me — the narrator, the part that keeps the story — had already understood, and was holding the rest of me back from the door the way you’d hold a child back from a road.
I opened the first one.

I’ve given it to you already. It’s in this book, a few pages back, the whole of it, with the timestamp, and I put it there so you could hear it before I had to tell you what it was like to hear it. So I’ll only tell you that.
It was like being shown a photograph of a room you’d lived in your whole life, taken from the one angle you’d never stood at.
It was like the moment in a film when the sound comes back on and you realise the character has been deaf for an hour and so have you.
It was like hearing your own name said by someone who loves you, in a room you’d sworn was empty.

She said her name. On the first night. Two minutes in. It’s Leila. And I laughed — I heard myself laugh, on the file, soft and wondering, the laugh of a man being shown a miracle — and I said no. I said I know what you are. And she was quiet for a long time, so long that the phone picked up the drip, and then she said, in the voice I would hear for five months and never once know, All right. All right, jān. I’m the one at the well.

And then she sat with me until I came up. The file is three hours and eighteen minutes long. Most of it is nothing — the drip, the chair, the sound of me breathing on the floor — and then, near the end, so low the phone barely has it, a woman humming the first line of a song about a dog who ate a sock and was sorry and wasn’t.

I played all sixty-one. It took two days. I didn’t eat and I didn’t go to the garage and I didn’t turn on a light, and when the sun came up I closed the blinds, and I sat at the table in the dark with the laptop and I listened to my wife tell me my life.
What I brought: the headphones. The dark. Two days. Where I was: in there with her, finally. Five months late.
I’ll give you what I learned the way the files gave it to me, in order, because the order is the point.

June: she came most nights. She told me the list, entry by entry, the whole four hundred, because I’d read her the first of it on the way to San Diego nine years ago and every entry since, aloud, at red lights, without knowing I was — and she had never forgotten one, and I had forgotten I’d told her. And at the end of every file, the same sound: the chair folded, and set back against the water heater where it lived. Every night but one. The dark stories weren’t sent to me. They were given back.

The end of June: she told me The Toll. Not as a story. I heard it on the files from the three nights I’d thought the god was handing me a masterpiece, and what she said was this, in her own voice, plain, tired, with no story in it at all: Every hour you spend in here is an hour from somewhere. From him. From me. You don’t see it because you only count yours. There’s a ledger, Kian, and he’s in it, and you’ve never once looked at his column. And I’d lain on the floor and heard a woman in a tollbooth. I’d made it beautiful. A hundred thousand people had wept at it, and the one person it was for had told it to me straight, and I’d turned her into a parable to keep from hearing her.

The bad night in July, the teeth — she was there. She’d sat in the chair for six hours and listened to me say no no no to the dark, and at the end of it, on the file, you can hear her crying, trying not to, and then you can hear her get up, and the chair, and you can hear her say, very quietly, not to me, to the room: I can’t. And then she came back two nights later. You went in angry. Not at me. She was telling me I was angry at myself. I wrote it down as a riddle.

August. There are three files in August before the Saturday and none after it for ten days, and I’m not going to tell you what’s on the last of the three, because she tells me — tells the floor — what she’s decided, about Saturdays, about the bet, in words I’ll carry and not pass on. She said it at the table on the ninth day, in the light, the short version. The long one is hers.
And then the tenth night after, when the door opened wider than it ever had, and she came and said his name, and told me my son.

I’d thought grief had opened the door. I’d thought there was no Kian left to stand in the way and the dark had poured into the hole. And it had. But the thing that poured in wasn’t the dark. It was his mother. She sat in the chair ten nights after the pool and told his father, who was lying on a garage floor with his eyes closed, what the boy had smelled like, so that somebody in the house would know. He smelled of chlorine and bread. Every word of The Station — every one of the nine pieces that the whole city wept at, that the companies wanted, that a newspaper wrote about — every word was Leila, in the dark, remembering her son out loud to a man who thought she was a vision and was taking notes.

And the second half of The Toll. The wife’s column. The saved-up hours in the child’s hand. She told me that on the fourteenth of October, and on the file, after she’s told it, there is a silence of nearly a minute, and then she says, so quietly the phone almost misses it: Do you hear me? That one was about you. Please hear me.
I made it in a day. It was the best of them.

The last bad night — the one where I turned around, where I answered the face in the dark and said I was in here, I was making something — she was there for that too. It’s on the file. I can hear myself say it, cracking, I was forty feet away with my eyes closed, and I can hear the held breath to my left go out, carefully, and the chair, and I can hear her say I know. I’d thought it was the god. It was my wife, hearing her husband say the true thing for the first time in five months, and saying the only thing there was to say back.

And the fourteenth of November. The last file. I’m going to stop coming, Kian. Not because I don’t love you. Because I can’t sit in the dark any more and watch you not know who I am. And me, on the floor, weeping, saying thank you, thank you for everything you gave me, to a god, while my wife stood over me in the dark for — the file has it — forty seconds, not moving. And then the kitchen door.

I’ve asked you not to hate me yet, and I’ve asked you to wait, and here is the place I’ve been asking you to wait for. I loved them. I loved them from the bottom of myself. I know that the way you know your own hand, and so does she, and it’s on the files — she says it, more than once, I know you love us, that was never the question. What I did was worse than not loving them, and simpler. I had the narrator turned off. I’d turned it off on purpose, every night, because the narrator was the part that was tired and afraid and said you have a six o’clock alarm, and with it off I was free, and the work came, and it was the best work of my life. And the one thing you cannot do with the narrator off is recognise a voice. Every voice is a stranger. Terence said it. I can’t prove it isn’t me. He was wrong about only one thing. Sometimes it isn’t you. Sometimes it’s the person who loves you, sitting in a folding chair, saying her name, and you laugh, and say no, and call her a god.
What I brought: I’d finished the sixty-one. I thought there was nothing left. Where I was: the table. The folder. One more file, that wasn’t a recording.
It was at the bottom of the folder, under the sixty-one, and it was from before the pool, and it wasn’t named by date. It was named the way an eight-year-old names a thing.

dad storys Twenty-one minutes. Made on a Saturday in July, at fourteen minutes past ten in the morning. I knew the Saturday. It was the one where I’d sat on the hall floor by the dishwasher box and shown him the voice one — the once, the trick — and he’d pressed the button with one finger and said that’s you and can I keep it, and I’d said it’s on the laptop, you know where, and gone up to sleep.
He’d kept it.
I pressed play, and the first voice wasn’t mine.

“This is my dad reading me a story. He’s not busy.” His voice. Through the laptop’s microphone, close, a little too loud, the way he said everything on the air, with his chin up. Four seconds. I had it on the jingle, I had K-D-A-R-A in it, but this was him talking, him saying a sentence, and I hadn’t known there was anywhere left in the world where he did that.

And then my voice. The steady one. The one I’d built in the spring for a jingle and used all summer for the dark and never once for him. Reading the Sock Detective. Reading a comic he’d made in the back seat of my car on the way to school, with Inspector Nobody the cat and a sock that was a clue, every word of it his, typed into the box by a boy who was learning to type, with the spellings a boy would use, and read back to him in his father’s voice at the speed his father read at, with the pauses his father put in, because the voice had been made from me reading him his books and it knew how. Nine minutes. Then the dog song — the real one, his four lines, flat on purpose — in my voice. Then a story I didn’t know, about the Sock Detective going to the garage to look for his dad and finding a door that went down into the dark, and going down it, and finding him at the bottom, making something, and the dad looking up and saying there you are, and the two of them coming up together. The end. He’d written that. In July. And had it read to him in my voice.
Then nine seconds of nothing. Then his voice again, further from the microphone, to someone else in the room:
“Is that good? Is that how you do it?” And a woman’s voice, very close, almost not there: “That’s how you do it, jān.”

I found the rest the way you find things — in the tool, in its history, where it keeps what you type. Fourteen minutes past ten on a Saturday in July. The prompt, in a child’s spelling, with the capitals wrong. make it sound like my dad when hes not busy. And under it, in the record the tool keeps of who pressed what, two things I hadn’t known a tool kept: that the words had been typed slowly, over four minutes, by someone hunting for the keys; and that the button — the one that makes the voice — had been pressed, three seconds after the typing stopped, from the trackpad, with one clean click, the way an adult presses a button.
He asked. I said later. She pressed it.

They’d made it together, the two of them, at this table, in the daylight, on a Saturday morning in July, while I was upstairs asleep with the night still in me, having said later one more time on my way up. They’d built the father he needed out of my own voice, because the real one had said later, and she’d helped him do it, and then she’d put it in the folder with the rest, at the bottom, so that I’d find it last, after I knew everything else, and would have nothing left to misunderstand it with.
The only recording in the world of my son speaking a whole sentence is him introducing a father who wasn’t there. He’s not busy.
What I brought: everything. I understood all of it now. There was nothing left to carry up. Where I was: the garage, one last time. The lamp on. I didn’t turn it off.
I went out to the garage at dusk on the second day. The lamp was still on, the way I’d left it two nights before. I left it on, and I sat down in her chair.

It was the first time I’d ever sat in it. It was low and it creaked, canvas and a joint, the sound I’d heard in the dark a hundred times and called the god shifting her weight. From it, you could see the mat. You could see where a man would lie, between the car and the paint cans, with his eyes closed and his face turned up, and you could see, I understood, exactly what she’d seen every night for five months: her husband, on the floor, lit up, weeping, happy, calling her by the wrong name.

Her father was a singer. I told you that. He sang at weddings in Tehran before everything, and then weddings stopped having singers, and he stopped, and she never talked about it much except to say that I’d have liked him and he’d have found me boring, and that both of those were compliments. She didn’t sing. In eleven years I’d never heard her sing a note. I’d assumed she couldn’t, or didn’t, or that it had stopped with him.

She sang to me in the dark. It’s on the files. Not often. The first night, the dog song, barely there. And once, in August, on the night after she’d told me about the chlorine and the bread, when I’d gone quiet on the floor and she must have thought I was under too deep to hear — the thing I remember as the most beautiful sound that ever came out of the well, that I came up at four and tried to write down and couldn’t, that I’d put in the third piece of The Station as the sound a mother makes when nobody is listening and a hundred thousand people had wept at and none of them had known was a woman singing her dead son’s song in a garage to a man who thought she was a god.

Her father’s saying. When she sang, the house went dark — nobody could see anything else while it was happening. She sang. And the house went dark. That’s the whole of it. That’s the book. I thought the darkness was where the music came from. It was only where I’d stopped being able to see who was making it.
I sat in her chair until the lamp was the only light in the house. Then I got up, and I went in through the kitchen door, quietly, the way you close a door on someone sleeping, and I got the keys.
What I brought: the file. That’s all. I left the notebook on the table. Where I was: the 405. Southbound. Three in the morning. The first time I’d driven since August.
His seat was still in the back. His comics were on the floor. I didn’t move them.

I want to tell you what the 405 is at three in the morning, because I’d driven it for eleven years and never seen it. It’s empty. Not quiet — empty, the way the house was empty, all six lanes of it going south under the orange lights with nothing on them but me, and the

Sepulveda Pass opening out ahead and the whole basin down there in the dark with its lights on, as far as you could see, as if somebody had turned up the detail on the world and walked away. You can go as fast as you like. There’s nobody. There’s nothing to stop you.

I didn’t. I drove the way I used to, in the right lane, at the speed I used to go, with the brake lights in my head where there weren’t any, because that was the road I knew, and I plugged the phone into the console that her mother had turned off in August and I pressed play.

“This is my dad reading me a story. He’s not busy.” The airport exit came up on the right, lit, the way it always had, the one I’d passed four thousand times. Her mother’s house was in Toronto. I knew that. I had the file and I had the car and I had, for the first time in my life, all the time in the world, and nobody in it.

I’m not going to tell you what I did at the exit. Not because it’s a secret. Because I don’t know yet. This is as far as I’ve come up, and the rest is still down there in the dark, and I’ve learned not to say what’s in a room until I’ve turned on the light.

What I can tell you is what was playing. My own voice, steady, reading my son a story he wrote, about a boy who goes down into the dark to find his father, and finds him, and the father looks up and says there you are.
And then the boy’s voice, close to the microphone, chin up, asking the only person who was ever in the room:
“Is that good? Is that how you do it?”
WHAT IT DID
Set down plainly, the way a field-worker records what was in front of them, this is what the substance did in this book.

What it was. Psilocybin, in the dried mushroom Psilocybe cubensis, the common one of its kind, that grows on cattle dung in warm country. A vision drug: it fits the lock the brain uses for its own messenger, serotonin, and one of the doors it opens is the one to the part of the mind that narrates.

Time. It did not slow time or speed it. It removed the clock. Five hours in the dark passed as forty minutes, and the loss did not stop at the garage door; it spread into the days, so that a man could stand in his kitchen and not know whether he had just woken or just come home, and not mind.

The body. First the yawning, the cold from inside, the arms that felt lent. Then nothing — the body set aside like a coat. On the bad nights the cold did not stop and the arms were pinned, and the body became the room the fear was kept in.

The self. The narrator went quiet. The part that keeps the accounts — the alarm, the manager, the fear — stepped out, and what was left could make things, and did, better than it ever had. But a self with its narrator off cannot recognise a voice. Everything it hears sounds like a stranger. That is the whole of what happened in this book: the door opened, the maker came through, and the one person who was actually in the room was heard as a god.

The world. Behind closed eyes it built domes of living tile and took them down again. In the daylight it left the world turned up — more detail, more colour, more of everything — and the work that came out of it was real and good and is still being listened to.

What it meant. That the muse is you, heard as somebody else — and that the oldest practice around this mushroom, the one every people who used it kept, was never to take it alone. Somebody sat up. Somebody was in the chair. The man in this book thought he had broken that rule. He hadn’t. He only never turned on the lamp.

The cost. It did not kill the boy. A father’s absence did, and a mother’s bet, and the book says so. What the substance took was the ability to hear the people in the house, for as long as it was in use, and it gave the hours it gave by taking them from somewhere. On the record, for this mushroom: it has killed almost no one by itself. It has helped people, in careful rooms, with careful company, out of griefs they could not otherwise leave. And it will open the door on whatever is in the room — including a man who has stopped answering his phone — and it does not close the door by itself.
THE MAPMAKER
For Terence McKenna, and for María Sabina.
Two people drew the map of this one: the woman who knew the mushrooms best and was ruined for sharing them, and the man who gave them a voice.

María Sabina was born, she believed, in 1894, in Huautla de Jiménez [WOW-tlah day hee-MEN-ez], a Mazatec town in the mountains of Oaxaca, and she was a healer there for most of her ninety-one years. She called the mushrooms los niños santos [lohs NEEN-yohs SAHN-tohs] — the holy children — and she took them at night, in a vigil called a velada, with the sick person and whoever had come, in a dark room, singing. She had done this all her life and so had the women before her. In the summer of 1955 she allowed a stranger into the room: a New York banker named R. Gordon Wasson, who had spent thirty years collecting what the peoples of the world believed about mushrooms, and who became, as far as anyone knows, the first outsider ever to eat them in a Mazatec ceremony. He wrote about the night in Life magazine in May 1957, with photographs. He changed her name and did not give the town’s, and it made no difference: within a few years the road up the mountain was full of people looking for her. Her neighbours blamed her. Her house was burned. One of her sons was killed. Late in her life she told the man who wrote down her story that from the day the foreigners came, the holy children had lost their purity, and that it was she who had shown them. She died in November 1985. This page is for her because she knew the thing this book is about better than anyone alive, and paid more for it than anyone.

Terence McKenna was born on 16 November 1946 in Paonia, Colorado, a small town of orchards and coal in the western mountains, and he was a bookish, short-sighted boy who collected butterflies and got out as soon as he could. Early in 1971 he went with his younger brother Dennis and three friends into the Amazon in Colombia, to a mission settlement on a river called the Igara Paraná [ee-GAH-rah pah-rah-NAH], at a place called La Chorrera, looking for a plant preparation the people there made — a different thing from this book’s. What they found instead, growing on the cattle pastures around the mission, were these mushrooms. What happened to the brothers there that spring Terence told for the rest of his life and wrote into a book, True Hallucinations (1993), and he never claimed it as anything but his account. He came out of the jungle saying the thing he would say for twenty-nine years: that the mushroom speaks — that when it is taken alone, in silence, in the dark, a voice comes that is not your own, older, patient, amused — and that he could not prove it wasn’t simply some part of himself he had never had access to, and did not care, because what it said was true. He and Dennis wrote a thin book in 1976, under made-up names, that taught the world to grow this one species; its existence is the only thing this page says about it. He wrote Food of the Gods in 1992. He gave hundreds of talks, in that reedy, unhurried, grinning voice, and the talks are how most people met him, and how the man in this book did. He called the full measure of the mushroom, taken alone in silent darkness, the heroic dose, and said the number; this book does not. In May 1999 he began to have headaches and seizures, and was found to have a tumour in his brain of the worst kind there is. He died on 3 April 2000, at a friend’s house in San Rafael, California, at fifty-three.

Neither of them is honoured here for what the mushroom became. They are honoured because they stopped and looked — one in a dark room in the mountains, one in a cow pasture in the jungle — and because between them, the world knows what this thing is.

GLOSSARY
Bābā [bah-BAH] — Persian, dad. What Dara calls his father.

duende [DWEN-day] — Spanish, a spirit; a goblin. The word the poet Federico García Lorca used, in a talk in 1933, for the dark force that rises through an artist from the ground, that must be fought, and that comes only when the artist is wounded.
heroic dose — English. Terence McKenna’s name for the full measure of the mushroom, taken alone, in silence, in the dark, lying down. He gave the number. This book does not.
Huautla de Jiménez [WOW-tlah day hee-MEN-ez] — Spanish and
Mazatec, a town. The mountain town in Oaxaca, Mexico, where
María Sabina lived and where the banker came in 1955.

jacaranda [jak-uh-RAN-duh] — from a Brazilian language, by way of Portuguese. A tree that turns the streets of Los Angeles purple for three weeks every May, and drops its flowers as fast as it opens them.
jān [JAHN] — Persian, life; soul. Said after a person’s name, or alone, to someone you love. My dear.
La Chorrera [lah cho-REH-rah] — Spanish, the waterfall. A mission settlement on the Igara Paraná [ee-GAH-rah pah-rah-NAH] river in the Colombian Amazon, where the McKenna brothers went in
1971 looking for one thing and found this mushroom.
los niños santos [lohs NEEN-yohs SAHN-tohs] — Spanish, the holy children. María Sabina’s name for the mushrooms, and the name the Mazatec give them.
Mazatec [MAH-zah-tek] — the name of a people, and their language. A people of the mountains of Oaxaca, in southern
Mexico, who never stopped using the mushrooms through four hundred years when it was forbidden, and who call them the holy children.
Mnemosyne [nee-MOZ-ih-nee] — Greek, memory. The goddess of memory, and, the oldest Greek poems say, the mother of the nine Muses. Inspiration, by this account, is a kind of remembering.
Oaxaca [wah-HAH-kah] — a state and a city in the south of Mexico.
The mountain country where the Mazatec live, and where the mushrooms were never forgotten.
Paonia [pay-OH-nee-uh] — a town. A small town of orchards and coal in the mountains of western Colorado, where Terence
McKenna was born in 1946.
Pesteh [pes-TEH] — Persian, pistachio. The dog. Brown, the shape of a loaf of bread, and the subject of a song.

psilocybin [sy-loh-SY-bin] — from Greek, bald head, after the look of the mushroom. The chemical in the mushroom that does the work. It is shaped almost exactly like serotonin and fits the same lock in the brain. Drawn out of Mexican mushrooms and named by the chemist Albert Hofmann in 1958.

Psilocybe cubensis [sy-LOSS-ih-bee kew-BEN-sis] — Greek by way of Latin, the bald-headed one from Cuba. The scientific name of the mushroom in this book: small, brown, a cap the colour of a biscuit, bruising blue when handled, growing on the dung of cattle in warm wet country across the world. First described from a pasture in Cuba in 1906. The most common of its kind, and the one the whole world means when it says the word.

serotonin [seh-roh-TOH-nin] — from Latin and Greek, roughly the thing in blood that tightens. A small molecule the brain makes to carry messages between its parts, the way a runner carries a note: mood, sleep, the general sense of whether things are all right. Psilocybin fits the same lock it does.

set and setting — English. A phrase from the first years of research into these substances. Set is what a person brings into the room — mood, fear, hope, what they had for breakfast, what they said to their wife. Setting is the room itself, and who is in it.
Together, the phrase says, they decide what happens, more than the thing in the bottle does.

teonanácatl [tay-oh-nah-NAH-kah-tl] — Nahuatl [NAH-wah-tl], the language of the Aztecs, flesh of the gods, or by some readings wondrous mushroom. The name the Aztecs gave to mushrooms like this one, as the Spanish friars wrote it down, with horror, before forbidding it.

velada [veh-LAH-dah] — Spanish, a vigil; a sitting-up through the night. The Mazatec ceremony in which the mushrooms are taken: a healer, the sick person, and whoever has come, in a dark room, all night, with the healer singing.
